title: PCB Layout Review
description: Layout review covering stackup, rules, mechanical fit, placement, power integrity, routing, specialized interfaces, safety spacing, EMC, test access and manufacturability.

items.text: Board outline matches the mechanical drawing, including dimensions and tolerances
items.hint: Overlay the DXF/STEP outline on the board outline layer and compare key dimensions. A wrong outline usually means a respin or a board that won't fit the enclosure.

items.text: Design rule check (DRC) runs with zero errors or every waived error is documented
items.hint: Run full online and batch DRC on the final database. Any waiver should name the rule, the location and why it's acceptable.

items.text: Layer stackup matches the fabricator's confirmed stackup (copper weights, dielectric thicknesses, materials)
items.hint: Get the stackup confirmed by the fab before routing impedance-controlled nets. Check the copper weight and dielectric thickness of every layer against the CAD layer setup.

items.text: Controlled-impedance trace widths and spacings match the stackup calculation
items.hint: Recalculate with the fab's dielectric constants or use their impedance report. Check every impedance class on every layer it's routed on.

items.text: Board material (FR-4 grade, Rogers, etc.) meets the electrical and thermal requirements
items.hint: Check Tg and Td against the reflow profile and operating temperature, and Dk/Df against the signal frequencies. Specify high-Tg material for lead-free reflow of thick or many-layer boards.

items.text: Stackup is symmetric about the board center
items.hint: Asymmetric copper or dielectric causes bow and twist after reflow. Mirror copper weights and dielectric thicknesses top to bottom wherever possible.

items.text: Every signal layer is adjacent to a solid reference plane
items.hint: A signal layer between two signal layers with no plane has no defined impedance or return path. If unavoidable, route those layers orthogonally and only with slow signals.

items.text: Power and ground planes that act as plane capacitance are on adjacent layers with thin dielectric
items.hint: Close-spaced power/ground pairs give low-inductance high-frequency decoupling. Confirm the intended pairs are adjacent in the stackup.

items.text: Impedance requirements and tolerances are stated on the fab drawing with layer and reference planes
items.hint: List each controlled-impedance class (e.g. 50 ohm SE, 90/100 ohm diff), the layer, the reference layers and the tolerance, so the fab can tune and test coupons.

items.text: Finished board thickness and tolerance match connector, card-edge and enclosure requirements
items.hint: Card-edge connectors, press-fit parts and slot guides need a specific thickness. Check the stackup total including plating and mask.

items.text: Outer-layer copper weight suits both the current and the finest pitch on that layer
items.hint: Heavy outer copper limits minimum trace/space and fine-pitch etching. Confirm with the fab's capability table for the chosen weight, e.g. 35 µm (1 oz) vs 70 µm (2 oz).

items.text: Surface finish (ENIG, HASL, OSP, ENEPIG, immersion silver) is specified and suits the parts
items.hint: Fine-pitch and BGA parts need a flat finish such as ENIG or OSP. Wire bonding and gold-finger contacts need specific finishes.

items.text: Design rules are set to the chosen fabricator's capability, not the CAD tool defaults
items.hint: Enter minimum track, space, drill, annular ring and mask rules from the fab's capability sheet for the selected class/price tier.

items.text: Net classes are defined for power, high-voltage, impedance-controlled and sensitive nets
items.hint: Net classes drive width, clearance and via rules automatically. Check that every special net is assigned to its class.

items.text: Clearance rules between net classes reflect the voltages present
items.hint: High-voltage nets need larger clearance to everything else. Set class-to-class rules so DRC catches violations instead of relying on visual checks.

items.text: Width rules for power nets are set from the current requirement
items.hint: Set minimum width per power net class from an IPC-2152 style calculation so thin necks are caught by DRC.

items.text: Differential pair rules (width, gap, uncoupled length) are defined for every pair class
items.hint: Without pair rules the router and DRC can't enforce coupling. Check the rules match the impedance calculation.

items.text: Length and match constraints are entered for timing-critical nets
items.hint: Enter match groups and tolerances from the interface spec or datasheet, then confirm the length report passes.

items.text: Schematic and layout are in sync, with no unresolved ECO differences
items.hint: Run a forward or back-annotation compare. Any difference means the board won't match the schematic that was reviewed.

items.text: Mounting holes are in the right positions with the right diameters for the fasteners
items.hint: Check hole positions and diameters against the mechanical drawing or enclosure CAD. Include tolerance on position.

items.text: Mounting holes are plated and grounded, or unplated and isolated, as the design intends
items.hint: Grounded mounting holes are often part of the EMC or ESD strategy. Isolated holes need copper keepout around the fastener and washer.

items.text: Copper keepout around mounting holes covers the fastener head, washer and standoff
items.hint: A screw head or metal standoff touching copper can short a net to chassis. Size the keepout to the largest hardware plus tolerance.

items.text: A 3D model check against the enclosure shows no collisions
items.hint: Export STEP with accurate component models and check it in the enclosure assembly, including lids, ribs, bosses and cables.

items.text: Component height limits are respected in every height-restricted zone
items.hint: Check tall parts (electrolytics, inductors, connectors) against the enclosure. Include the board-to-lid gap and any tolerance stack.

items.text: Connectors line up with the enclosure openings, including position and height tolerance
items.hint: Check the mating face against the panel cut-outs. A connector that is off by a fraction of a mm may not mate through the opening.

items.text: LEDs, buttons, light pipes and displays line up with their enclosure features
items.hint: Check positions in the 3D assembly. Light pipes need the LED centered under them, and buttons need the right actuator height.

items.text: Board-edge clearance suits the routing, V-score or breakout method
items.hint: Copper and parts too close to a V-score or tab can crack or get damaged. Use the fab and assembler's edge-clearance rules.

items.text: Keepouts for heatsinks, shields, clips and enclosure ribs are drawn and respected
items.hint: Mechanical parts that are not in the BOM are easy to forget. Add them as keepout regions so DRC catches conflicts.

items.text: Mechanical layers carry the fab and assembly drawings with dimensions, notes and datums
items.hint: The fab needs a dimensioned outline with a datum. Check that the drawing on the mechanical layer matches the current outline.

items.text: All components are inside the board outline with adequate clearance to the edge
items.hint: Use the assembler's edge clearance, especially if the board travels on conveyor rails. Parts too close to a breakout tab can crack when depaneled.

items.text: Bypass capacitors are placed as close as possible to the IC power pins they serve
items.hint: Put the smallest-value capacitor nearest the pin with the shortest possible loop to ground. Check in the layout, not just by reference designator.

items.text: High-dissipation components have enough copper area to spread their heat
items.hint: Compare the copper area under and around each hot part with the datasheet's recommended thermal layout.

items.text: Sensitive analog parts are physically separated from noisy digital and switching circuits
items.hint: Group by function and keep switching nodes, clocks and fast digital away from high-impedance analog inputs.

items.text: Connectors face the right way for their mating direction and assembly
items.hint: Check pin 1 and the mating face in 3D against the cable or mating board. A mirrored connector is a respin.

items.text: Mechanical constraints (keepouts, mounting holes, standoffs) are respected
items.hint: Check every placed part against the keepout regions on the mechanical layers.

items.text: Polarized parts and ICs are in a consistent, verified orientation
items.hint: Keep the same orientation for like parts where possible to make inspection easier. Check every diode, electrolytic and IC pin 1 against the footprint.

items.text: Every footprint matches the datasheet land pattern for the exact orderable part
items.hint: Check pad size, pitch, pin numbering and package variant. Use IPC-7351 style land patterns or the manufacturer's recommendation.

items.text: Components are placed in functional groups that follow the signal flow
items.hint: Grouping by function shortens critical routes and keeps noisy and quiet circuits apart.

items.text: Crystals and oscillators are next to their IC, away from board edges and noisy circuits
items.hint: Keep crystal traces short with ground beneath and no signals routed under the crystal. Follow the IC's layout guidance for load capacitors.

items.text: Switching regulators are placed per the datasheet layout example
items.hint: The datasheet layout keeps the hot loop small. Moving the input capacitor or inductor away from it can cause noise and instability.

items.text: Parts are placed to allow rework access, with room around BGAs and fine-pitch parts
items.hint: Rework nozzles and soldering irons need clearance. Tall parts right next to a BGA block rework.

items.text: Bottom-side parts suit the assembly process
items.hint: Heavy or tall parts on the bottom may fall off during second-side reflow or need glue. Confirm with the assembler which parts can go on the bottom.

items.text: Through-hole parts are placed for the chosen soldering method (wave, selective or hand)
items.hint: Selective solder nozzles need clearance around pins. Wave soldering needs SMD parts on the bottom oriented and spaced for the wave.

items.text: Heat-sensitive parts are kept away from hot components
items.hint: Electrolytic capacitors, crystals, batteries and sensors drift or age faster near regulators and power resistors.

items.text: Parts near board edges or V-score lines are oriented to reduce flex cracking
items.hint: Ceramic capacitors near edges or depanel lines can crack. Orient them parallel to the break line and keep them back from it.

items.text: Each decoupling capacitor connects to the power and ground planes through short, wide paths
items.hint: Mounting inductance dominates at high frequency. Use short traces from pad to via, and vias placed beside or inside the pad.

items.text: Decoupling capacitors have their own vias rather than sharing vias with the IC pin
items.hint: Shared vias increase the current loop. As a rule of thumb, give each capacitor its own via pair where space allows.

items.text: Bulk capacitance is placed where each rail enters a region or a high-current load
items.hint: Bulk capacitors handle lower-frequency load steps. Put them at the regulator output and near large loads.

items.text: Voltage drop from regulator to load is within the load's tolerance at maximum current
items.hint: Estimate IR drop through traces, planes and vias, or run a DC drop analysis for high-current rails.

items.text: Remote sense lines take a Kelvin connection at the load point
items.hint: Route the sense pair together, away from the high-current path and switching nodes.

items.text: Regulator feedback traces are short and kept away from the switch node and inductor
items.hint: Noise coupled into the feedback node causes jitter and instability. Route it on the quiet side of the circuit with a ground reference.

items.text: Switching regulator hot loops (input capacitor, switch, return) are as small as possible
items.hint: The input loop carries the fastest current edges. Keep it tight on one layer with the input capacitor close to the switch pins.

items.text: Switch-node copper is no larger than needed to carry the current
items.hint: A large switch-node area radiates. Keep it compact and do not route sensitive signals under or next to it.

items.text: Power delivery network impedance meets the target for processor, FPGA or memory rails
items.hint: Use the vendor's PDN tool or a simulation to check impedance vs frequency against the target from the datasheet.

items.text: Power and ground planes are solid, with minimal splits or voids
items.hint: Look at each plane layer on its own. Rows of vias with large anti-pads can cut a plane as badly as a deliberate split.

items.text: Plane connections to pads and vias use the intended thermal relief or direct connection
items.hint: Thermal relief helps soldering on through-hole and large pads. High-current or thermal paths may need direct connections instead.

items.text: Ground stitching vias tie ground layers together around the board and between layers
items.hint: Stitch ground pours to the ground plane so islands don't float, and consider a via fence along the board edge. Spacing is a rule of thumb set by the highest frequency of concern.

items.text: Plane-to-plane capacitance is used where it helps the power delivery network
items.hint: Tightly coupled power/ground planes add low-inductance capacitance. Worth checking on dense, fast digital boards.

items.text: Where split analog and digital grounds are used, they join at a single, deliberate point
items.hint: Most modern designs use one solid ground with careful placement instead of split grounds. If grounds are split, check no signal crosses the gap and the tie point is where the datasheet recommends.

items.text: Copper pours have no unconnected islands
items.hint: Floating copper can act as an antenna. Remove islands or stitch them to ground with vias.

items.text: Plane necks between regions are wide enough for the current they carry
items.hint: Narrow plane necks create hot spots and voltage drop. Check every place a pour narrows between vias or around cut-outs.

items.text: Power planes are pulled back from the board edge relative to ground
items.hint: Rule of thumb: pull power planes back from the board edge relative to the ground plane to reduce edge radiation (often called the 20H rule). Treat this as guidance, not a hard limit.

items.text: Each power island is large enough and connected with enough vias for its current
items.hint: Count vias at each layer transition of high-current rails. Via current capacity depends on plating thickness and diameter.

items.text: All nets are fully routed, with no unrouted connections
items.hint: Check the unrouted-net report is empty. Watch for plane connections that DRC treats as connected but are actually cut off.

items.text: Differential pairs are routed symmetrically with matched lengths
items.hint: Keep both traces of a pair together with equal length and the same via transitions. Check the match tolerance against the interface spec.

items.text: Fast signals have a continuous reference plane beneath them
items.hint: Check every layer a fast signal uses, including after layer changes. A gap in the reference raises impedance and radiation.

items.text: Return current paths are not interrupted by plane splits or via anti-pads
items.hint: Look for anti-pads merging into slots under signal routes, especially in connector and BGA fields.

items.text: Trace widths carry their current with margin for the allowed temperature rise
items.hint: Size from IPC-2152 style charts using the actual copper weight and allowed rise. Inner layers run hotter than outer for the same width.

items.text: Crosstalk-sensitive traces have enough spacing from aggressors
items.hint: Rule of thumb: 3W spacing (three times the trace width, center to center) for sensitive or fast signals. Use simulation for tight designs.

items.text: Fast signals use as few vias as possible
items.hint: Each via adds a discontinuity and stub. Plan layer assignment to reduce layer changes on fast nets.

items.text: Fast signals have no trace stubs
items.hint: Stubs from unused branches, test pads or T-junctions cause reflections. Route daisy-chain or fly-by, or keep stubs very short.

items.text: Traces have no acute angles
items.hint: Acute angles can trap etchant and narrow the trace. Use 45 degree or curved bends.

items.text: Clock traces are short, point-to-point and away from board edges and I/O
items.hint: Clocks are a common emission source. Route them on inner layers between planes where possible.

items.text: Adjacent signal layers are routed orthogonally or with planes between them
items.hint: Parallel routing on adjacent layers causes broadside coupling. Check layer pairs with no plane between them.

items.text: Traces entering pads leave from the pad end or center, not at an angle across the pad
items.hint: Off-center or wide traces into small pads cause tombstoning and uneven solder. Keep entry width at or below the pad width.

items.text: Sensitive traces are not routed under noisy parts such as inductors, crystals or switch nodes
items.hint: Magnetic and electric fields couple into traces directly underneath. Check the layers beneath every switching part.

items.text: Long parallel runs between aggressor and victim nets are avoided
items.hint: Coupled length matters as much as spacing. Check long buses and traces that share a channel.

items.text: Unused copper fragments and dangling traces are removed
items.hint: Leftover stubs act as antennas and confuse later revisions. Run the dangling-track check.

items.text: High-speed nets are routed on layers with the impedance defined in the stackup
items.hint: Check each high-speed net only uses layers with a calculated geometry for its impedance class.

items.text: Intra-pair skew compensation is placed near where the mismatch occurs
items.hint: Compensating at the far end leaves the pair skewed along most of its length. Use small serpentines near the bend or pin that causes the mismatch, and check the result against the interface spec.

items.text: Pair-to-pair length matching meets the interface spec where required
items.hint: Some interfaces (e.g. parallel lanes with a forwarded clock) need lane-to-lane matching. Others tolerate skew. Follow the spec or IC guide.

items.text: Differential pairs stay tightly coupled, with uncoupled length kept to a minimum
items.hint: Breakouts at pins and around vias are the usual uncoupled sections. Keep them short and symmetric.

items.text: Spacing between differential pairs is enough to keep crosstalk acceptable
items.hint: Rule of thumb: keep pair-to-pair spacing several times the intra-pair gap. Simulate or follow the IC's layout guide for dense routing.

items.text: Each high-speed signal via has a ground return via next to it
items.hint: Ground vias beside signal vias keep the return path close at layer changes. For pairs, place them symmetrically.

items.text: Via stubs on multi-gigabit links are back-drilled or avoided by layer choice
items.hint: Long via stubs cause resonances. Route to layers that leave short stubs, or specify back-drilling on the fab drawing.

items.text: AC coupling capacitors are placed per the interface spec, with matched pads and no stubs
items.hint: Place both capacitors of a pair side by side. Consider a reference-plane cut-out under large pads to control impedance, per the IC guide.

items.text: Pad and connector transitions are designed to keep impedance close to target
items.hint: Large SMT pads and connector pins are capacitive. Use anti-pads or plane cut-outs per the connector or IC layout guide.

items.text: Serpentine length tuning uses spacing and segment lengths that avoid self-coupling
items.hint: Tight serpentines couple to themselves and shorten the effective delay. Rule of thumb: keep serpentine spacing at least a few trace widths.

items.text: Fiber weave effect is addressed on long, fast differential pairs
items.hint: Pairs running parallel to glass fibers see skew. Route at a slight angle, use spread glass, or follow the fab's advice for the data rate.

items.text: Loss budget for each long high-speed channel is within the interface spec
items.hint: Long traces on standard FR-4 may exceed the insertion loss budget. Estimate or simulate loss for the longest channels.

items.text: DDR routing follows the memory controller vendor's layout guidelines
items.hint: The SoC or FPGA vendor's layout guide sets topology, length rules and stackup. Check every rule against the layout.

items.text: Data byte lanes are routed on the same layer group as their strobe
items.hint: Keep each DQ/DM byte lane and its DQS pair together, with the same number of vias, so they track over temperature.

items.text: Data-to-strobe length matching within each byte lane meets the vendor tolerance
items.hint: Check the match group report per byte lane. Include package pin delays if the vendor requires it.

items.text: Address, command and control nets are matched to the clock within the vendor tolerance
items.hint: Check the address/command group against CK in the length report.

items.text: Address and command routing uses the specified topology (fly-by or T-branch)
items.hint: DDR3 and later normally use fly-by for multiple devices. Check the device order matches the write-leveling setup.

items.text: Fly-by termination resistors are at the end of the chain with short stubs
items.hint: Place VTT termination after the last memory device and keep stubs from the main route short.

items.text: VTT and VREF are routed and decoupled per the layout guide
items.hint: VREF should be a quiet, well-decoupled trace away from aggressors. VTT needs a low-impedance plane or wide trace with local capacitors.

items.text: Memory signals have a continuous reference plane with no splits beneath them
items.hint: Check under the full length of every DDR net, including the breakout regions under the controller and memory.

items.text: Memory clock pairs are routed as controlled-impedance differential pairs
items.hint: Check width, gap and intra-pair skew of CK pairs against the vendor's rules.

items.text: Spacing between byte lanes and between data and address groups meets the guide
items.hint: Crosstalk between groups closes the timing eye. Follow the vendor's group-to-group spacing.

items.text: RF traces are routed as controlled-impedance lines with the geometry from the stackup
items.hint: Check width and gap for microstrip or coplanar waveguide against the calculation for the RF layer and its reference.

items.text: Antenna placement and keepout follow the module or antenna datasheet
items.hint: Antennas need specific copper-free areas, board-edge position and ground plane size. Copy the reference layout closely.

items.text: No copper, components or traces sit inside the antenna keepout on any layer
items.hint: The keepout applies to every layer, including ground pours. Check internal layers as well as the outer ones.

items.text: Matching network footprints are placed close to the antenna feed or RF pin
items.hint: Leave room for a pi or L network even if parts are not fitted, so the antenna can be tuned on the final board.

items.text: RF traces have no sharp bends
items.hint: Use curved or mitered bends. Keep RF traces short and avoid vias in the RF path unless designed for it.

items.text: Coplanar ground beside RF traces is stitched with a dense row of vias
items.hint: Rule of thumb: space stitching vias a small fraction of a wavelength apart along RF lines. Follow the RF IC's layout guide where it gives a value.

items.text: RF ground plane under the radio IC and RF path is solid and unbroken
items.hint: Do not route other signals through the RF reference layer under the RF section.

items.text: Radio IC exposed pad has the recommended number of ground vias
items.hint: The exposed pad is often the RF ground and the main thermal path. Follow the datasheet via pattern.

items.text: Shield can footprint, if used, is continuous and well grounded
items.hint: Shield frames need a solid ground ring with stitching vias. Check that tall parts fit under the can.

items.text: Digital and switching circuits are kept away from the RF section and antenna
items.hint: Clocks, DC-DC converters and display interfaces can desense the receiver. Keep them physically separate.

items.text: RF test connector or test point footprint is provided for conducted measurements
items.hint: A switched RF connector or a pad for a pigtail makes conducted power and sensitivity tests possible for certification and debug.

items.text: High-impedance analog inputs are short and kept away from digital and switching traces
items.hint: Picoamp or high-gain inputs pick up coupling easily. Route them on the shortest path with ground on either side.

items.text: Guard rings surround high-impedance input nodes where leakage matters
items.hint: Drive a guard at the same potential as the input to cut surface leakage. Leave it out of the solder mask if the datasheet suggests it.

items.text: Current sense resistors use Kelvin connections
items.hint: Take sense traces from the inside edges of the resistor pads, routed as a pair, so the measurement excludes the solder joint and trace resistance.

items.text: ADC and DAC reference pins are decoupled at the pin with short loops
items.hint: Reference noise feeds straight into the conversion result. Place the reference capacitor as close as the datasheet shows.

items.text: Analog and digital sections of each ADC/DAC are placed per the datasheet
items.hint: Place the converter so analog pins face the analog section and digital pins face the digital section.

items.text: Differential analog inputs are routed as a symmetric pair
items.hint: Matching length and environment keeps common-mode rejection. Route both traces together over the same reference.

items.text: Thermal gradients across precision parts are minimized
items.hint: Heat sources near references, thermocouples or matched resistors cause drift. Keep matched parts together and away from hot parts.

items.text: Sensitive analog nets are not routed beneath digital buses or switching regulators
items.hint: Check every layer beneath the analog path, not only the top layer.

items.text: Audio input and output grounds return to the intended point
items.hint: Speaker and headphone return currents can modulate the input ground. Route high-current audio returns separately from input references.

items.text: High-current paths have enough copper width or area for their current
items.hint: Check every high-current path, including through connectors, fuses and switches, against IPC-2152 style data for the copper weight used.

items.text: Vias carrying high current are numerous enough for the load
items.hint: Each via carries limited current. Use multiple vias at layer changes and check against plating thickness.

items.text: Power stage component placement keeps high di/dt loops small
items.hint: Place half-bridge FETs, the DC-link capacitor and gate drivers so the commutation loop is as small as possible.

items.text: Gate drive traces are short and routed with their return
items.hint: Route gate and source return as a pair to reduce loop inductance and ringing.

items.text: Thermal vias are placed under exposed pads and hot components
items.hint: Use the datasheet's thermal via pattern. Specify via fill or tenting if solder wicking into open vias is a concern.

items.text: Thermal reliefs are not used where a part relies on the copper for heat sinking
items.hint: Spokes reduce heat transfer. Hot parts often need solid connections even if soldering takes more heat.

items.text: Heatsink and thermal-pad contact areas are free of tall parts and solder mask where needed
items.hint: Exposed copper or a flat area may be needed for a thermal pad or clip-on heatsink.

items.text: Current shunts and their Kelvin traces are placed away from heat sources
items.hint: Shunt resistance changes with temperature. Keep sense traces away from the high-current path.

items.text: Connectors and terminal blocks are rated and placed for the current, with wide copper to each pin
items.hint: Spread current across all connector pins assigned to the rail. Thin traces to a connector pin are a common hot spot.

items.text: Battery connection traces can survive a short circuit until the protection trips
items.hint: Battery short-circuit current can be very high. Check the copper and fuse withstand the energy before the protection acts.

items.text: Creepage between isolated circuits meets the applicable safety standard on every layer
items.hint: Take values from the applicable standard's tables for the working voltage, pollution degree and material group. Measure along the surface, including around slots.

items.text: Clearance through air between isolated circuits meets the applicable safety standard
items.hint: Clearance is measured in a straight line through air. Include parts that overhang the board and the enclosure.

items.text: Isolation barrier is clear of all copper, vias and pours on every layer
items.hint: Check internal layers. A pour or via inside the barrier on any layer defeats the isolation.

items.text: Isolation slots are used where creepage cannot be met on the surface
items.hint: Slots increase creepage distance. Check the slot width and position against the requirement and fab capability.

items.text: Isolating components (optocouplers, transformers, isolators) straddle the barrier
items.hint: Check that the component's own creepage and the board creepage both meet the requirement.

items.text: Primary-side and secondary-side components are clearly grouped on each side of the barrier
items.hint: A part from one side placed on the other is an easy error. Mark the barrier on silkscreen or the assembly layer.

items.text: Mains input traces, fuses and protection parts have the required spacing to each other and to chassis
items.hint: Include spacing between line and neutral as well as to protective earth. Use the applicable standard's tables.

items.text: Protective earth connections are sized and fastened as the safety standard requires
items.hint: Earth connections often need specific copper area and fastening. Check with the safety engineer.

items.text: High-voltage areas are marked on the silkscreen
items.hint: A warning symbol or outline around hazardous voltage areas helps during test and service.

items.text: ESD protection devices are placed at the connector, before any other component
items.hint: The ESD path should go from connector pin to protection device to ground with the shortest possible trace. Route the protected signal through the device pad.

items.text: ESD protection has a short, low-inductance connection to ground
items.hint: Use multiple vias directly at the ground pad of the protection device.

items.text: I/O connector shields connect to chassis or ground as the grounding plan intends
items.hint: Check the shield connection: direct, through a capacitor, or through an RC network. Follow the system grounding plan.

items.text: Filters on I/O lines are placed at the connector
items.hint: Common-mode chokes and ferrites only work if they sit between the noise source and the cable.

items.text: Noisy circuits are kept away from I/O connectors and cables
items.hint: Cables act as antennas. Keep clocks and switching regulators away from the connector area.

items.text: Chassis ground and signal ground are separated or joined as the grounding plan intends
items.hint: Check the chassis pour, gap and any bridging capacitors match the plan.

items.text: Exposed metal (buttons, connectors, screws) has an ESD discharge path that avoids sensitive circuits
items.hint: An ESD strike must flow to ground without passing near sensitive ICs. Check the path from each user touch point.

items.text: Reset and other sensitive control lines are kept short and away from board edges
items.hint: ESD and fast transients can trigger resets through long traces. Add filtering near the IC pin if they must be long.

items.text: Footprints for optional EMC parts (ferrites, capacitors, RC snubbers) are provided on risky nets
items.hint: Spare footprints let the team fix EMC problems at pre-compliance testing without a respin.

items.text: Bend regions have no vias, pads or components
items.hint: Vias and pads in a bend crack with flexing. Keep them in rigid or stiffened areas.

items.text: Bend radius meets the fab's guidelines for the flex thickness and layer count
items.hint: Bend radius depends on flex thickness and whether the bend is static or dynamic. Use the fab's design guide.

items.text: Traces in bend regions run perpendicular to the bend line
items.hint: Traces at an angle to the bend line take uneven strain. Route straight across the bend.

items.text: Traces on adjacent flex layers are staggered, not stacked, through bends
items.hint: Stacked traces form an I-beam that stiffens the flex and concentrates stress.

items.text: Ground planes in flex areas use hatched copper where flexibility is needed
items.hint: Solid copper stiffens the flex. Check that a hatched plane still gives the needed impedance and shielding.

items.text: Pad and trace junctions in flex areas use teardrops or fillets
items.hint: Teardrops reduce stress at the junction and help coverlay adhesion.

items.text: Stiffeners are defined with material, thickness and position on the drawing
items.hint: Stiffeners under connectors and components need to be on the fab drawing, with adhesive type.

items.text: Rigid-to-flex transitions keep copper features away from the transition line
items.hint: The transition zone sees the most stress. Follow the fab's keepout from the rigid edge.

items.text: Coverlay openings are sized and positioned per the fab's guidelines
items.hint: Coverlay openings are less accurate than solder mask. Check the fab's minimum opening and registration tolerance.

items.text: Flex outline has radiused internal corners and tear-stop features
items.hint: Sharp internal corners on flex tear easily. Add radii and copper tear-stops at slits.

items.text: BGA fanout pattern follows the package vendor's recommended via and escape strategy
items.hint: Check the vendor's escape routing guide for via size, pad size and number of layers needed.

items.text: BGA pad type (solder mask defined or non-solder mask defined) matches the vendor recommendation
items.hint: Pad type affects joint reliability. Use the package datasheet.

items.text: Dog-bone vias are fully covered or plugged so solder doesn't wick away from the ball
items.hint: Open vias next to BGA pads can steal solder. Tent, plug or mask them per the assembler's advice.

items.text: Via-in-pad is filled and plated over (capped) where used
items.hint: Open via-in-pad wicks solder and causes voids. Specify filled and capped vias on the fab drawing.

items.text: Microvia aspect ratio and stacking are within the fab's capability
items.hint: Stacked microvias can be less reliable than staggered ones. Check the fab's rules for stacking and aspect ratio.

items.text: Sequential lamination build-up is described clearly on the fab drawing
items.hint: Show which layers each microvia and buried via spans, with drill tables per span.

items.text: Power and ground balls have enough vias to the planes
items.hint: Share vias between balls only if the vendor allows it. Check the current per via.

items.text: Decoupling capacitors under the BGA are placed and connected per the vendor's guide
items.hint: Bottom-side capacitors under a BGA need short via connections to the power balls.

items.text: Unused BGA balls are handled as the datasheet requires
items.hint: Some unused balls must be tied to ground or left floating. Check the pin list.

items.text: Pin 1 is marked clearly for every IC and connector
items.hint: The mark should be visible after the part is placed, not hidden under the body.

items.text: Reference designators are readable and placed next to their parts
items.hint: Use a consistent orientation, with at most two reading directions.

items.text: Silkscreen text size meets the fab's minimum line width and height
items.hint: Text below the fab's limits smudges. Use the fab's minimum values.

items.text: Board name, part number and revision are on the silkscreen or copper
items.hint: Every board should be traceable. Copper text survives harsh processing better than silk.

items.text: Space for a serial number or barcode label is provided
items.hint: Leave a clear area for a label or laser marking, sized for the label or code.

items.text: Connector pin functions and voltage markings are on the silkscreen where users connect cables
items.hint: Mark supply inputs with voltage and polarity, and mark user-wired terminals.

items.text: Regulatory and safety markings required on the board are present
items.hint: Some products need certification marks, UL recognition or warning symbols on the PCB. Confirm with the compliance plan.

items.text: Test points, jumpers and debug headers are labeled
items.hint: Labels speed bring-up and test. Use net names or short descriptions.

items.text: Test points are provided for all critical signals and power rails
items.hint: Every power rail, reset, clock and key interface should be probe-able on the assembled board.

items.text: JTAG/SWD/debug header is accessible with the board installed
items.hint: Check access in the enclosure. A debug port that needs disassembly slows bring-up and field debug.

items.text: In-circuit test (bed-of-nails) access is maintained for all testable nets
items.hint: Agree the test strategy with the contract manufacturer. Missing access means untested nets in production.

items.text: Polarity markers are visible on the silkscreen for all polarized components
items.hint: Check every diode, LED, electrolytic and tantalum capacitor. The marking must be visible after assembly.

items.text: Test points are on one side of the board where the fixture design requires
items.hint: Single-sided fixtures are cheaper. Put all test points on the side the fixture probes.

items.text: Test point size and spacing meet the test fixture's probe requirements
items.hint: Use the test house's minimum pad size and pitch. Small pads cause unreliable contact.

items.text: Test points are kept clear of tall components
items.hint: Probes need clear access. Tall parts nearby block probes and fixture plates.

items.text: Programming and debug connectors are placed for both bench and production use
items.hint: Consider a pogo-pin pad pattern for production programming in addition to a bench header.

items.text: Ground test points are near each group of signal test points
items.hint: Short ground leads are needed for clean scope measurements.

items.text: Zero-ohm links or jumpers are provided to isolate rails for bring-up
items.hint: Breaking a rail lets you measure current and isolate faults during bring-up.

items.text: Minimum trace width and spacing are within the fabricator's capability
items.hint: Compare against the capability sheet for the copper weight on each layer. Finer features usually cost more.

items.text: Minimum drill size and aspect ratio are within the fabricator's capability
items.hint: Aspect ratio is board thickness over drill diameter. Check against the fab limit for through vias and microvias separately.

items.text: Annular ring is sufficient for all vias and plated through-hole pads
items.hint: Set annular ring per fab capability and the IPC-6012 class ordered. Drill wander eats into small rings.

items.text: Solder mask slivers between pads are eliminated
items.hint: Slivers below the fab's minimum web flake off. Gang-relieve fine-pitch pads if the web cannot be held.

items.text: Courtyards and silkscreen do not overlap pads or conflict with adjacent parts
items.hint: Overlapping courtyards mean parts will collide. Run the courtyard check and the silk-to-pad check.

items.text: Fiducial marks are present on each populated side for automated assembly
items.hint: Use global fiducials on the board or panel, and local fiducials near fine-pitch parts if the assembler asks. Keep a clear mask opening around them.

items.text: Tooling holes are present and correctly sized for panelization
items.hint: Use the assembler's tooling hole size and position, usually on the panel rails.

items.text: Solder mask dams between fine-pitch pads meet the fab's minimum
items.hint: Mask dams prevent solder bridges. Check the dam width against the fab capability.

items.text: Solder mask expansion is set per fab capability
items.hint: Too small and mask may encroach on pads, too large and adjacent pads merge. Use the fab's registration tolerance.

items.text: Via tenting, plugging or filling is specified on the fab drawing
items.hint: State which vias are tented, plugged or filled. Partially tented vias can trap chemicals.

items.text: Copper has no acid traps
items.hint: Acute angles between traces trap etchant. Most CAD tools have a check for this.

items.text: Copper has no slivers below the fab's minimum width
items.hint: Thin copper slivers from pours can lift and short. Set a minimum pour width and remove slivers.

items.text: Copper is balanced across each layer and between layers
items.hint: Uneven copper causes warp and plating thickness variation. Add copper thieving in empty areas if the fab agrees.

items.text: Panelization is agreed with the assembler, including rails, breakaway method and panel size
items.hint: Check the panel drawing with the assembler. Parts near tabs or V-scores need extra clearance.

items.text: Paste layer is correct, including paste reduction on large pads and exposed pads
items.hint: Exposed pads usually need a windowed paste pattern to avoid voids and float. Follow the datasheet or assembler's advice.

items.text: Gerber, drill and fab drawing outputs have been checked in a Gerber viewer
items.hint: Generate from the final database, then check every output layer. Confirm drill files match the drill table.

items.text: IPC-6012 class and acceptance criteria are stated on the fab drawing
items.hint: State Class 2 or Class 3 as the product needs. This drives annular ring, plating and inspection.
